q: How is the c in cantik (pretty) pronounced?
why: c is always ch in Indonesian, never k or s.

q: The letter e has two sounds. How do you know which one a word has?
o: Learn it with the word: the pronunciation line shows eh or uh
It is always the uh sound
An e at the start of a word is always eh
There is no difference: both sound the same
why: The spelling writes both sounds as e, so learn each word's e from the pronunciation line.

q: How do you end the word tidak (not)?
o: With a popped k, as in English kick
With a catch in the throat, like the break in uh-oh
Drop the k and stretch the a
why: A final k is a catch in the throat; it is never popped.

q: It's 4 p.m. and still light. Which greeting fits?
why: sore runs from about 3 p.m. until dark; malam starts after dark.

q: A friend says Selamat tahun baru! (Happy New Year!). What do you say back?
why: Return a wish by repeating it with juga (too); sama-sama only answers thank you.

q: How do you say My name is Emma?
why: Nama saya is literally name my: nama comes first, saya after it.

q: Which word means both he and she?
why: dia covers he and she; Indonesian does not mark the difference.

q: Your friend's father greets you. What do you call him?
why: An older man gets the title Bapak, or Pak when you speak to him.

q: You tell a hotel clerk that you and your wife come from the US. Which we?
why: kami leaves the listener out; the clerk is not part of your family.

q: How do you ask a stranger's name?
why: Names are asked with siapa (who), and the owner Anda comes after nama.

q: How do you say I'm 25 years old?
why: Age is said as my age, 25 years: umur saya dua puluh lima tahun, never with punya.

q: Which sentence means I'm from America?
why: Before a place phrase Indonesian needs no word for am: Saya dari Amerika.

q: How do you say I'm tired?
why: A describing word follows the person directly: Saya capek.

q: Where does adalah belong?
o: Between two noun phrases, in careful speech
why: adalah links two noun phrases; it is never used before an adjective or a place.

q: Kemarin saya makan. means Yesterday I ate. What shows the past?
o: Nothing: it can only mean now
why: makan never changes; kemarin (yesterday) shows the time.

q: How do you say this book?
why: ini comes after the noun in a phrase: buku ini.

q: What does Ini teh. mean?
why: With ini first, the words make a sentence: This is tea.

q: Kopi itu panas. means…
why: kopi itu is that coffee, and panas after it says what it is like: That coffee is hot.

q: How do you say a new car?
why: The describing word comes after the noun: mobil baru.

q: Which one means That house is big?
why: When besar comes after itu, it says something about the house: a full sentence.

q: Where does sangat (very) go?
o: At the start of the sentence
why: sangat goes before the adjective (sangat besar); sekali goes after it (besar sekali).

q: How do you say Budi's house?
why: The owner comes after the thing: rumah Budi.

q: What does bukunya mean?
o: his or her book, or the book
why: -nya is his, her, its or their, and it can also work like the.

q: my friend's car =
why: Each owner follows what it owns: mobil, then teman, then saya.

q: How do you ask Whose car is this?
why: The thing comes first and siapa takes the owner's place: mobil siapa.

q: Where are you going? (to a friend)
why: Going somewhere takes ke mana; di mana asks where something is.

q: How do you turn Kamu lapar (You're hungry) into a question?
o: Say it with a rising voice
why: A rising voice is enough; Apakah at the start is the careful written form.

q: How do you say "I'm not a teacher"?
why: guru is a noun, so the negative word is bukan, placed right before it.

q: Which word goes before lapar (hungry) to say "not hungry"?
why: lapar is a describing word, so it takes tidak.

q: Your friend points at a car and asks Itu mobil kamu? It isn't yours. The short answer is…
why: The question is about a noun (your car), so the short no is Bukan.

q: How do you say 100?
why: se- means one in front of a block: seratus.

q: How is Rp15.000 read?
why: The dot marks thousands, and belas makes the teens: lima belas ribu.

q: "two big houses" =
why: The number goes before the noun and the describing word after it: dua rumah besar.

q: setengah tiga is…
why: setengah counts toward the next hour: half way to three is 2:30.

q: jam tiga means…
why: jam before the number means o'clock; tiga jam would be three hours.

q: Which question asks the time?
why: Jam berapa? is "what time?"; Berapa jam? asks how many hours.

q: "There's a pharmacy near here." =
why: ada means there is; adalah only links two noun phrases.

q: You ask a receptionist Ada kamar kosong? There are none. The answer is…
why: There isn't any is tidak ada.

q: Dia di rumah and Dia ada di rumah…
o: the second means she has a house
why: ada before a place is optional: both say where she is.

q: "I'm going to Bali." =
why: Going somewhere takes ke.

q: "Where are you going?" (to a friend) =
why: Where to is ke mana.

q: Which is spelled correctly for "at home"?
why: di before a place is a separate word: di rumah.

q: adik means…
why: adik names the age, not the sex: any younger sibling.

q: Someone asks Sudah menikah? You're single. The expected answer is…
why: Belum (not yet) is the expected answer; Tidak sounds blunt.

q: "my older brother" =
why: kakak first, then laki-laki, then the owner: kakak laki-laki saya.

q: "I haven't eaten yet." =
why: Not yet is belum, the time word placed before the verb.

q: Which word means "right now, in the middle of doing"?
why: sedang marks something in progress.

q: Which word means "still"?
why: masih means still: Dia masih di kantor.

q: "to work" (the ber- verb) =
why: kerja takes be-, not ber-: bekerja.

q: Which one is a ber- verb?
why: berenang (swim) is a ber- verb; membaca takes me-.

q: Saya kerja di Jakarta is…
o: fine in casual speech; careful speech says bekerja
why: Dropping ber- is normal casual speech; the full form is bekerja.

q: baca + me- =
why: Before b the prefix is mem-: membaca.

q: tulis + me- =
why: t drops after men-: menulis.

q: kirim + me- =
why: k drops after meng-: mengirim.

q: How do you say 'I want to go'?
why: mau goes straight before the verb, with no word for 'to'.

q: Which question asks for permission: 'May I come in?'
why: boleh is about permission: Boleh saya masuk?

q: What does Saya tidak bisa datang mean?
why: bisa is about being able to, so tidak bisa is 'can't'.

q: How do you say 'Don't go!'?
why: Commands with 'don't' use jangan; tidak only describes.

q: Which is the polite way to ask a waiter for an iced tea?
why: minta + a thing means 'may I have'.

q: Your host says Silakan duduk. What is she doing?
why: silakan offers or invites: please, go ahead.

q: How do you say 'the person who lives here'?
why: yang comes right after the noun, then the description.

q: Pointing at some shirts, what does Yang merah mean?
why: yang + a describing word on its own means 'the … one'.

q: Which is correct for 'the book I bought yesterday'?
why: A longer description needs yang, even where English drops 'that'.

q: How do you say 'The room has been booked'?
why: di- goes on the root and is written as one word: dipesan.

q: What is the di- verb of membeli (to buy)?
why: Take off meN- to get the root beli, then add di-: dibeli.

q: Which spelling is right for 'eaten at home'?
why: The di- verb is joined; di before a place is a separate word.

q: How do you say 'This one is cheaper'?
why: lebih goes before the describing word, which never changes.

q: What does paling enak mean?
why: paling means 'most, -est'.

q: How do you say 'too expensive'?
why: terlalu means 'too'; sangat only means 'very'.

q: How do you say 'Turn right'?
why: belok is turn, and kanan is right.

q: What is a perempatan?
why: perempatan has four ways; a T-junction is a pertigaan.

q: What does Apoteknya di seberang bank mean?
o: The pharmacy is across from the bank.
The pharmacy is next to the bank.
The pharmacy is behind the bank.
The pharmacy is inside the bank.
why: di seberang means 'across from'.

q: How do you say 'I get up at six'?
why: jam before the number is the clock time; enam jam would be six hours.

q: What does mandi mean in daily life?
o: a long soak in a bathtub
washing yourself, usually a shower or scooped water
why: mandi is the everyday wash, not a long bath.

q: Where is bargaining with Bisa kurang? normal?
o: at a minimarket with price tags
why: Bargain at markets and street stalls, not where prices are printed.

q: How do you say 'three books'?
why: The number already shows the plural, so the noun is not repeated.

q: What does buku mean on its own?
o: book or books, depending on the situation
why: Plural is usually not marked: buku can be one or many.

q: Which repeated word is NOT a plural?
why: kupu-kupu just means butterfly; the word only exists repeated.

q: What is the standard form of nggak?
why: nggak and enggak are the casual forms of tidak.

q: Who can you call lo?
o: a Jakarta friend your own age
why: gue and lo are only for Jakarta friends your own age.

q: Which message suits an email to your teacher?
why: Writing to a teacher calls for standard forms: saya, belum, selesai.
